title: RAG Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Night-before revision notes on retrieval-augmented generation: why RAG, chunking, embeddings and indexing, hybrid search, reranking, context assembly with citations, and the failure modes that break it.

chapters.title: What RAG Is and the Mental Model
points: RAG = retrieve relevant text at query time, put it in the prompt, and have the LLM answer from it; the model weights stay unchanged
Two phases: offline ingestion (load, clean, chunk, embed, index) and online query (embed query, retrieve, rerank, assemble, generate)
RAG vs fine-tuning: RAG injects fresh or private facts and can cite sources; fine-tuning changes style, format or skill, not reliable facts
RAG vs long context: stuffing everything costs more per query, slows responses and degrades recall for details in the middle; retrieval keeps the prompt small
Mental model: answer quality is capped by retrieval quality, so the LLM can only be as right as the chunks it receives

chapters.title: Chunking Strategies
points: A chunk is the unit that gets embedded and retrieved; too big dilutes the embedding, too small loses context
Fixed-size chunking (e.g. 500 tokens) is simple but cuts sentences and ideas mid-way
Recursive splitting tries paragraph, then sentence, then word separators, so it keeps natural boundaries and is the usual default
Overlap of 10-20% (e.g. 500 tokens with 50-100 overlap) stops facts on a boundary from being lost, at the cost of a larger index
Structure-aware chunking splits by headings, code blocks or table rows; attach metadata (source, title, section, date) to every chunk

chapters.title: Embeddings and Indexing
points: An embedding maps text to a dense vector so that similar meaning gives nearby vectors; similarity is usually cosine or dot product
Use the same embedding model for documents and queries; changing the model means re-embedding the whole corpus
Exact (flat) search compares against every vector; approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes trade a little recall for big speed gains
HNSW is a graph-based ANN index with high recall and fast queries but heavy memory; IVF clusters vectors and searches only the nearest clusters; tune ef_search or nprobe for recall vs latency
Store vectors with metadata in a vector DB (pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, OpenSearch) and apply metadata filters like tenant, date or doc type before or during search

chapters.title: Hybrid Search and Reranking
points: BM25 is keyword scoring by term frequency and rarity; it wins on exact terms like IDs, error codes and names, while vectors win on paraphrase and meaning
Hybrid search runs BM25 and vector search in parallel and merges the two ranked lists
Reciprocal Rank Fusion scores each doc as sum of 1/(k+rank) across lists (k is about 60), so it needs no score normalization
Retrieve wide then rerank: fetch top 50-100 candidates cheaply, then score the query-document pairs with a cross-encoder reranker and keep the top 3-8
Bi-encoders embed query and doc separately, which is fast and scales; cross-encoders read them together, which is more accurate but too slow to run on the whole corpus

chapters.title: Context Assembly, Citations and Failure Modes
points: Context assembly: dedupe near-identical chunks, order by relevance, keep within a token budget, and label each chunk with an ID like [1] and its source
Prompt rules: answer only from the provided context, cite chunk IDs, and say 'I don't know' when the context lacks the answer
Citations: have the model output chunk IDs, then map them back to source URL or page and verify each cited ID was actually in the context
Retrieval failures: bad chunking, vocabulary mismatch, missing metadata filters, stale index, and the right chunk ranked below the cutoff
Generation failures: hallucinating beyond the context, ignoring middle chunks (lost in the middle), and contradictory chunks; diagnose by checking retrieval recall first, then answer faithfulness

chapters.title: RAG Cheat Sheet
points: Pipeline: load, clean, chunk, embed, index | query, retrieve, rerank, assemble, generate, cite
Chunking defaults: recursive split, 300-800 tokens, 10-20% overlap, metadata on every chunk
Retrieval defaults: hybrid BM25 plus vectors, fuse with RRF (k=60), top 50 candidates, rerank to top 5
Evaluate separately: retrieval (recall@k, MRR) and generation (faithfulness, answer relevance)
Fix order for bad answers: check chunks, then retrieval recall, then reranking, then the prompt
